title: CYSTINOSIS, LATE-ONSET JUVENILE OR ADOLESCENT NEPHROPATHIC TYPE

relationships.phenotype: CYSTINOSIS, LATE-ONSET JUVENILE OR ADOLESCENT NEPHROPATHIC TYPE

intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that late-onset juvenile or adolescent nephropathic cystinosis is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the CTNS gene.

checks.claim: Late-onset juvenile or adolescent nephropathic cystinosis is caused by homozygous mutation in the CTNS gene.
checks.evidence_quote: The disease occurs due either to the combination of one mild mutation and one which is known to cause nephropathic cystinosis or to homozygosity for a predicted mild mutation.
checks.explanation: The abstract names homozygosity for a mild CTNS mutation as one cause of intermediate cystinosis. 'Intermediate' is a synonym for the late-onset juvenile/adolescent form.

checks.claim: Late-onset juvenile or adolescent nephropathic cystinosis is caused by compound heterozygous mutation in the CTNS gene.
checks.evidence_quote: The disease occurs due either to the combination of one mild mutation and one which is known to cause nephropathic cystinosis or to homozygosity for a predicted mild mutation.
checks.explanation: One mild mutation combined with one nephropathic mutation is compound heterozygosity in CTNS.

paragraphs.text: Late-onset (juvenile or adolescent) cystinosis is a rarer form of cystinosis than the infantile nephropathic form. Symptoms begin between 12 and 15 years of age (Attard et al., 1999), and renal failure can develop (Langman et al., 1985). Goldman et al. (1971) compared the adolescent form with the infantile and adult forms of cystinosis.

paragraphs.text: Thoene et al. (1999) and Attard et al. (1999) established autosomal recessive inheritance of intermediate cystinosis. Thoene et al. (1999) found that patients were either compound heterozygous or homozygous for mutations in the CTNS gene.

checks.claim: Intermediate cystinosis shows autosomal recessive inheritance.
checks.evidence_quote: The disease occurs due either to the combination of one mild mutation and one which is known to cause nephropathic cystinosis or to homozygosity for a predicted mild mutation.
checks.explanation: Biallelic mutations imply recessive inheritance, but the abstract never says 'autosomal recessive' explicitly.

checks.explanation: The abstract states both the compound heterozygous and the homozygous mechanisms.

paragraphs.text: Thoene et al. (1999) identified CTNS mutations in 6 patients with intermediate cystinosis. Two of the mutations had not been reported before. In these patients the disease resulted either from compound heterozygosity for one mild mutation and one mutation known to cause nephropathic cystinosis, or from homozygosity for a predicted mild mutation. Transfecting cystinotic fibroblasts with normal CTNS cDNA partially corrected the cells' phenotype. Transfecting them with a cDNA carrying a mutation that causes intermediate cystinosis did the same.

paragraphs.text: Attard et al. (1999) screened the CTNS gene in 3 groups of patients: those with infantile nephropathic cystinosis, those with late-onset cystinosis, and those whose phenotype did not fit the classical definitions. They found 23 different CTNS mutations, 14 of them novel. In 2 patients with late-onset cystinosis, the mutations affected regions of cystinosin that are not functionally important. The authors concluded that this accounted for the milder phenotype.

paragraphs.text: Attard et al. (1999) studied 25 patients with infantile nephropathic cystinosis. Twelve had 2 severely truncating CTNS mutations, consistent with loss of functional protein. The other 13 had missense mutations or in-frame deletions predicted to disrupt transmembrane domains and abolish protein function. Three other patients had onset of cystinosis before 7 years of age but a milder course than the infantile nephropathic form, and they carried CTNS missense mutations. The authors suggested that these mutations allow production of functional protein and may mark regions of cystinosin that are not functionally important.
